title: Stephen A. presses Roger Goodell on the NFL’s biggest issues while in Brazil 🏈 | NFL on ESPN
text: Commissioners, good to see you, sir. How you doing? How's everything going? >> Everything's great. We're here in Rio. How could it be any better? >> You're right about that. Cowboys Ravens being here at Makana Stadium. What does it mean for the NFL's long-term plans in Brazil? Well, you know, our initiative is to be a global sport and um Brazil's got 38 million NFL fans today and we think there's a great deal of potential to expand that and bringing two, you know, great franchises like the Ravens and the Cowboys is is going to be, I think, electric here in Rio. First time in Rio. Two years prior we were in S Paulo. And the fans here are just um they love sports. uh they're mad about sports and um they really embrace it with with a real flavor. >> You've spoken adamantly about, you know, the NFL extending to to to Europe and basically globally at all. How plausible is that? How soon do you see that transpiring particularly in Europe in terms of potentially adding another NFL team? >> Well, adding a team and and you know, expanding our efforts are two different things for us. Um, you know, we think we can play 16 regular season games. We're continuing to push flag football on a global basis. 20 million kids playing it, boys and girls around the world. And it's creating more engagement. These games create a spark in the market. Um, our media partners are obviously critical to what we do, our sponsors, our licensing business, which you're proudly wearing today, which I'm happy to see. But all of that's giving people another way to interact with the NFL and to touch the NFL. Um eventually if we continue to grow the way we've been growing, you know, I can see an international franchise. I don't know what the time frame is, but we're not rushing that. We want to make sure we're right and we continue the growth pattern. >> What do you need to see specifically in order for you to make that decision down the line? you know, just the growth in the markets and and frankly, we're having so much interest from so many markets on a global basis, Stephen. So, we we got to look at this and sort of say >> what are the best markets for us to be in. >> Yeah. >> Um so, a lot of this is for us to >> sort of understand what's got the strongest fan base, what's has the great stadiums, uh what has the great media and uh sponsorship base. Those are things that ultimately are going to probably um be the determining factors. Ultimately, >> getting specifically into this game, Dallas is hosting uh the Ravens, the Baltimore Ravens here in Brazil. There's been some complaints about the field. Uh we've heard from the NFL PA talking about there was some concerns or what have you. You assured everybody that's not going to be a concern. Everything will be ready. When you think about that, what field standard must the Monak Monaco stadium meet for safety and performance amid the NFL PA's concerns? >> You know, Stephen, a the complaints that you've heard were for the soccer players um that were playing on this field and and so they have a different barometer, a different standard. Theirs is about the ball rolling smoothly on a grass field, right? >> That's not our issue. Our our issue is stability in it. Uh proper footing. Um and they're two different things. We saw that in the World Cup. And so what we're working uh with the players association, but also with all of our partners, is trying to improve the technology both for grass and artificial fields and make it consistent. Uh we think the big thing is consistency in the field so the players can adjust from player from practice to games. And when you go into a different market, you're having one game here. Um and what we've had is our experts down here, uh they're confident in the ability of the field to to hold up in a an NFL standard and that's what we're going to continue to work toward. >> Commissioner, when I think about a game here, for example, Brazil, you know, from New York, it took it took about 10 hours to get here and and it's a long flight. It's worth it. Please don't get me wrong. It's worth it, but it was still a long flight. When you think about players and the concerns they have as it pertains to safety, travel does play a role in all of that. H how, you know, when you think about players and their complaints or their concerns in regard to that, what do you say to them? What's the kind of mindset that you have? >> We actually we don't wait for that. We we seek it. We we're looking for input. What are those important things? When we were Australia two weeks ago, >> we spent a lot of time talking about that. What's the right thing? The teams chose different patterns on when they would arrive and when they would uh where they would train. Um, so all of this is something where you you're learning as you go and you're trying to understand what's the best ways best way to prepare uh for the game and what's the best way to recover which is a big factor. How how quickly do they recover? What is it? And you know we've played in Brazil now this is our third year Australia. Um we're learning more about how to do that. When we play in Europe a lot of times the teams from the west coast play on the east coast and then go over. So, uh, I think we've been able to do that effectively, but you can always get better at it and we're going to continue to look at that. >> What I would imagine that you've learned some things from the whole Rams 49ers experience continue considering the different paths that both teams took. The San Francisco 49ers were there a week earlier and it showed. The Los Angeles Rams arrived 28 hours before kickoff and it showed. I mean, so I I'm asking what I mean, is that self-explanatory in its own way? I don't know because you know we have teams in the first week that didn't play well um and it didn't have anything to do with travel back in the states. So you know you know the question ultimately is you know is a team ready to play. Is that just because of the travel and and just because I don't know that. Uh I think the Rams know that better than any of us ultimately. >> Um and you know we'll we'll obviously have time to share with that. Um but you know everyone's going to choose a different approach. They're all trying to out compete and outsmart the other guy and that's something that you encourage ultimately. But I think we did learn something in the travel even even the fact that somebody a team could land the day before and play in Australia the day and leave and get back um basically when almost when the game started. >> Uh so you know when you look at that you're talking about a real quick turnaround. >> I don't know if that's the best way but I I think uh maybe there's something in between. What can we do to make sure that they're protected when they're in that defenseless position? Um, in a quarterback situation, they have a lots of that protection. >> But when they get outside of that, >> they have to learn to use the rules and recognize now you're a runner. And these guys are great athletes, great runners. they can do just about anything out there and defenders come and say, "Hey, listen. You want to try to tackle them?" And they're out there and they're they're freelancing. And so at that point in time, you're now a runner. And you lose a lot of that protection. So quarterbacks need to learn to use and they h I think they do, but they need to learn that to use that protection. Um but that that is something that um you're going to get those things. Um, but you also want to hear from the offensive player and you want to hear from the coaches and you want to make sure that you're balancing that in a way that it's going to lead to the best competition but the safest possible game. >> Let me transition to the issue of gambling and and it's relevant because it's so prevalent in the world of sports more so than ever before at least over the last several years. But it's a competitive we we're averaging eight to 10 changes a year. Yeah, Stephen. So, it's >> it's a it's a tough job. title: Coach Saban Breaks Down College Football Week 4 with Pat McAfee
text: This is the greatest college football coach of all time. AJ uh Nick Sab. >> Coach, how you doing? Can you hear them? >> Doing great. Can hear them fine. >> Okay. Did you hear Rap sheet? What are your thoughts on him? Ian Rapaort. He said you loved him. >> Yeah, I loved him. He was full of when he covered me and he's still FULL OF [laughter] >> WHOA. >> YES. >> Junior have a feelood. >> He he he was good. And it's no surprise to me that, >> you know, he's done really well in the business because he was objective and uh he was always fair. Uh and I I always appreciated that. >> Yeah. It feels like you have no idea who Raph. >> Would you read stuff, coach? [laughter] Would you read stuff? Would they bring it to you? Like would would your PR people bring you stuff that was written about your team and would you actually read it? >> No. >> Really? Never. Ever. You would never hear what the outside noise is. Did somebody come and like tell you like, hey, this is kind of what is being said about the team right now, so maybe the team is hearing this. Is that the type of stuff how you would hear about it? >> Yeah. And they would tell me things that I needed to know that were happening that I might get asked about. But I I I tried to stay away from the good and the bad, whatever was being written, because I didn't really want it to affect, you know, like what I was trying to do with the team. But I used to use the media a lot in terms of my press conferences and the message that I sent to the media and I was really talking to the team. >> Oh yeah. >> So I was trying to use them >> to your point about the rat poison that people have cuz when you lose your edge in this game um man you get bad quick. So, um, it was always a fight, especially when you were dealing with success to to keep people on edge so that they had the intensity that you needed to be able to play well. >> That's what they were just talking about, the let down game. And AJ, uh, AJ, you and I have talked about this plenty of times, and we're pretty similar humans, I do believe. You know, we don't need the rahrh speeches and all that type of We we're not really into that. But we never fully understand. Like, I would have a bad day and I didn't know why. Like, I had no idea why I was having a bad day. Now, now my preparation was everything. Warm-up was good, and for some reason, I just can't hit a damn ball. A there's some games, I think, where AJ thought he was going to be fantastic and then he had a bad game. And we wonder whenever we're looking at other teams, it's like, do coaches know like if their team's going to have a bad game or is that come from nowhere? Cuz there's a lot of potential let down games. I mean, Miss obviously has the biggest opportunity to fall off of a climactic volcano that they were on top of last week down there in Oxford, but it's like, how do you judge and how do you figure out whether or not your team is about to maybe fall off a cliff before we even know cuz I don't even think players know at that time. >> Yeah. Well, I think that's one of the most difficult things to do when you're a coach is to try to get a feel for where your team is and because we had weeks where we would really practice well and prepare well and then be flat as a pancake when the game >> and then we had other g times when I am just pulling my hair out because practice is not very good, people are not very focused and then we would get to the game and really play pretty well. So, uh, it's just so hard to figure out. But I think that, you know, from a psychological standpoint, what I was always trying to do is get the people to have the right sort of psychological disposition of what you had to do to be successful on a consistent basis and try to get them to buy into that and not give these raw speeches and emotional things to try to get people up and down because that doesn't really last. You know, you got to have the competitive character in inside of you to always take the next challenge and always try to be the best that you can be. And you know, that's not normal. I mean, normal is do what you got to do to get by. I mean, we all made an A on the first test, screwed around for two weeks, made a C on the next one, and get a B average, and we're happy about that, right? I mean, that ain't how you win a championship. That's not how you be the best you can be, but that's normal. >> See, I started at C at the top there, F. And then you see there's a D and they say D's get you to be eligible for the [laughter] bowl game. >> That's all I needed out there. But I understand what you're saying about relief syndrome. I I believe is the way you've potentially described it before. Let's talk about some relief syndrome potentially. And the color the the orange is bright. I mean, it's like you're walking out of a casino at like 6:00 a.m. Now, I'm not saying that you've been there all night. Hopefully, you're winning.
